analysis.title: Mid-term Elections Preview Part 4
key_insights: With US mid-terms next week, Natixis reviews approval ratings, House and Senate battleground maps, economic conditions in swing districts and the policy implications of a divided Congress.
Republicans hold a 53-47 Senate majority and a 217-212 House majority (1 independent, 5 vacancies). All 435 House seats and 35 Senate seats are up in November.
President Trump's approval rating is around 38%, and issue-specific approval (foreign policy, economy, inflation, immigration) continues to decline.
Trump's approval among non-MAGA Republicans fell from around 75% to roughly 10%, while approval among MAGA Republicans stayed near 90%. Natixis expects this to dampen Republican turnout.
The Democrats' generic ballot lead has widened and the Right Track/Wrong Track polls show worsening perception of the country's direction.
Since WW2 the president's party has lost 25 House seats on average in mid-terms, and has lost seats in 18 of the last 20 mid-term elections.
Democrats look well positioned to win the House. Securing the Senate is harder but possible. Democrats need a net gain of four Senate seats because VP Vance breaks 50-50 ties.

Since the August update, Senate ratings shifted toward Democrats overall: Kansas moved from likely Republican to toss-up, Texas and Iowa from lean Republican to toss-up, Alaska and Michigan from toss-up to lean Democratic, and North Carolina, Georgia and New Hampshire from lean to likely Democratic.
Some ratings moved toward Republicans: South Carolina from lean to likely Republican, Mississippi from likely to safe Republican, and Minnesota from likely to lean Democratic.

As of October 27 there are 11 safe, 3 likely and 1 lean Republican Senate seats. Democrats must defend 9 safe, 3 likely and 3 lean Democratic seats and capture at least two of five true swing states (Texas, Kansas, Ohio, Iowa, Maine).

Only about 46 of 435 House seats are truly contested per 270towin.com. Unemployment is above the US average in more of the 46 districts, while inflation is in balance with the national average. Economic indicators are not materially worse in contested districts.

Texas Senate (Talarico D vs Paxton R) is a toss-up, with Talarico holding a narrow lead in recent polls. Ohio (Brown D vs Husted R), Iowa (Turek D vs Hinson R), Maine (Jackson D vs Collins R) and Kansas (Hamilton D vs Marshall R) are also toss-ups.
Kansas became competitive on dissatisfaction with tariff policies and higher diesel prices hitting agriculture. Cook and Sabato rate it toss-up (10/20), Decision Desk lean Republican.

Alaska (Peltola D vs Sullivan R) and Michigan (El-Sayed D vs Rogers R) are lean Democratic, though Cook still rates both toss-up. North Carolina (Cooper D vs Whatley R) and Georgia (Ossoff D vs Collins R) are likely Democratic.
Trump administration priorities on immigration, trade and foreign policy sit with the executive branch, so their direction is not expected to shift dramatically after the election.

In a divided government Natixis is fairly confident (absent a recession) there will be no huge new spending program, but expects marginally more fiscal pressure as Democrats push to reinstate spending cut by the One Big Beautiful Bill.

Democratic votes would be needed to fund the government, avoid a shutdown and raise the debt ceiling. Natixis expects Democrats to use this leverage to try to roll back healthcare and food assistance cuts.

On immigration, a Democratic Congress would most likely constrain the administration through DHS funding negotiations rather than pass sweeping reform. The CBO projects population growth to fall, with a large decline in net immigration of other foreign nationals.

On trade, Congress has delegated tariff authority to the president and is unlikely to claw it back. Reversing tariffs over a presidential objection requires legislation plus a signature or a two-thirds Senate veto override.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Weak presidential approval correlates with losses for the president's party in mid-terms.

risk_factors: A recession could change the expectation of no large new spending program under divided government.
Democratic use of funding leverage could raise shutdown and debt ceiling risk.
Broad discontent with the state of the economy should weigh on incumbent parties regardless of local conditions.
